Public Resolutions
pub'lik rez-ō-loo'shunz
n. pl. (the resolutions of the Commission of the Scottish General Assembly, 1650–51, admitting former Engagers to the defence of the kingdom)
public, from Latin publicus, of the people; resolution, from Latin resolutio, a loosening, a determination.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Public Resolutions were the answers given by the Commission of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, in December 1650 and again in 1651, to a question put by the Committee of Estates after Cromwell had destroyed the Scottish army at Dunbar: whether men excluded from public trust by the Act of Classes — the Engagers of 1648 and the followers of Montrose — might now be employed in the defence of the kingdom. The Commission answered that in such extremity they might. The reasoning was that the invasion threatened the very existence of the covenanted nation, that necessity permitted the use of any hand that would fight, and that the alternative was conquest. The answer split the Church of Scotland in two. Those who accepted it were the Resolutioners; those who protested against it were the Protesters, and the breach was never healed before the Restoration swept both away. The question was not whether the men were needed but whether a covenanted church may employ those it has judged unfit. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines necessity as that which makes an act unavoidable, and a resolution as a formal determination of an assembly.

expand to see more

NECES'SITY, n. That which makes an act or event unavoidable; compulsion; irresistible force.

RESOLU'TION, n. A formal determination of a public body or assembly; a fixed purpose.

EN'GAGER, n. One who engages or binds himself; in Scottish history, a subscriber of the Engagement of 1648.

EXTREM'ITY, n. The utmost point; the highest degree; the most pressing distress.

Key Scripture

Zec 4:6 — "Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."

Jdg 7:2 — "And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me."

Jdg 7:3 — "Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand."

1Sa 14:6 — "And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few."

Modern Corruption

The 1650 answer on employing excluded men, which split the Church of Scotland.

expand to see more

The argument from necessity that carried the Public Resolutions is perpetually available and perpetually dangerous. It is the reasoning by which churches in every generation suspend their own standards for an emergency: the cause is just, the danger is real, the help is needed, and the rule can be kept again afterwards. There was no afterwards. Within a decade the men whom the Resolutions readmitted, or men of their party, were the government that drove the covenanted ministers out of their parishes.

The principle to recover is that God's cause is not advanced by numbers and is not lost for want of them, which is the whole lesson of Gideon's army: “The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands” (Jdg 7:2). Jonathan states the same from the other side: “for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6).

Usage

"“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — the answer the Protesters gave."

"“The people that are with thee are too many for me” (Jdg 7:2) — against the argument from numbers."

"“there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6) — after Dunbar."
